about: Twelve apostles and twelve martyrs. Paul stands among the apostles in place of Matthias — Rome counted the college its own way. The martyrs are five popes (Linus, Cletus, Clement, Sixtus, Cornelius), Cyprian the bishop of Carthage, Lawrence the deacon, and after them Chrysogonus, John and Paul, Cosmas and Damian. The name of St Joseph was put here by John XXIII in 1962 — the one change he made to the Canon. The whole sentence is one chain of genitives hanging from memóriam venerántes, and the opening participles find no main clause of their own: either a verb is supplied in thought, or — as others read it — they reach back to the offerers named in the Memento just before, and the prayer's own petition arrives only in “concédas” near the end.

s01.translation: In communion with, and venerating the memory first of all of the glorious ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of our God and Lord Jesus Christ:

s02.translation: and also of blessed Joseph, Spouse of the same Virgin,

s03.translation: and of Thy blessed apostles and martyrs, Peter and Paul, Andrew, James, John, Thomas, James, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon and Thaddeus:

s04.translation: of Linus, Cletus, Clement, Sixtus, Cornelius, Cyprian, Lawrence, Chrysogonus, John and Paul, Cosmas and Damian:

s05.translation: and of all Thy Saints; grant, for their merits and prayers, that in all things we may be defended by the help of Thy protection.

s07.translation: Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

w001.function: A nominative plural participle whose subject the sentence never states: the priest and those who stand with him — or, on another reading, the offerers named in the prayer just before.

w004.function: A deponent participle: passive in form, active in meaning. The whole chain of genitives that follows hangs from it.

w009.function: Semper Vírginis — ever Virgin: the adverb wedged between adjective and noun, as in the Líbera nos: beáta et gloriósa semper Vírgine.

w011.function: Genetríx is she who bears; the whole Dei Genetríx is the Latin for the Greek Theotókos, the word settled at the Council of Ephesus.

w019.function: “sed et” is the fixed phrase for and furthermore — not an adversative but a widening of the list.

w021.function: An indeclinable name: only “beáti” (w020), which agrees with it, shows the case.

w024.function: A genitive in apposition to “Ioseph” (w021): with the name indeclinable, the case shows in beáti and in Sponsi.

w029.function: A genitive plural in the chain hanging from “memóriam”; Whitaker's reads a phantom singular here and is set aside by ruling — hence the disputed flag on this word.

w033.function: Paul stands here in the place of Matthias: the Roman list counts twelve, but not the twelve that Acts counts.

w035.function: The first of the two Jameses — the brother of John, son of Zebedee.

w038.function: The second James, son of Alphaeus; Latin distinguishes them by nothing but their place in the line.

w045.function: Here the second twelve begins: martyrs of Rome, or martyrs Rome honoured in its own churches.

w047.function: The name means merciful — the same word the Canon’s opening line carries as clementíssime.

w049.function: Cornelius, pope (251–253) — the fifth and last of the popes in this series.

w050.function: The bishop of Carthage — the only one in this list who is not a saint of Rome; the rest Rome honoured as its own.

w055.function: Not the apostles named above: a Roman pair of martyrs, with a church of their own on the Caelian hill.

w058.function: Physician brothers; neither of the dictionaries the corpus checks its forms against carries their names, so the parse here rests on the chain of genitives alone.

w064.function: An ablative read as cause: for their merits. The bare form allows means as well — by their merits, as received translations often take it.

w066.function: A subjunctive used as a petition: may thou grant.

w069.function: Neuter: in all things, not among all men.

w070.function: From tégere, to roof over; a protéctio is a roof held out above someone.

w072.function: From mœnia, city walls: the image is not a shield but a wall built round a city.

w073.function: An ablative of means closing the prayer; its verb muniámur stands wedged inside the phrase itself: protectiónis tuæ … auxílio.

w075.function: “The same”, because Christ has already been named at the head of the prayer; where he has not, the Canon says simply Per Christum.
